paragraphs.heading: A wave made by displacement
paragraphs.text: A tsunami is a series of waves in a body of water, generally an ocean or a large lake, caused when a large volume of water is displaced. That sets it apart from the sea’s other movements. Normal ocean waves are generated by wind. Tides are generated by the pull of gravity from the Moon and the Sun. What generates a tsunami is water being displaced in a large event.

paragraphs.heading: What sets one off
paragraphs.text: The displacement is usually caused by earthquakes. Landslides, volcanic eruptions and glacier calvings can also be the cause, and more rarely meteorites and nuclear tests, though whether a meteorite can cause a tsunami is debated. Much is still unknown. One major area of current research asks why some large earthquakes generate no tsunami while other, smaller ones do.

paragraphs.heading: What it looks like
paragraphs.text: Tsunami waves do not look like normal sea waves, since they have a far longer wavelength. A tsunami may not appear as a breaking wave at all and may at first resemble a rapidly rising tide. Tsunamis generally arrive as a series of waves called a “wave train”, with periods ranging from minutes to hours. Large events can generate wave heights of tens of metres.

paragraphs.heading: A name that never quite fits
paragraphs.text: The word is borrowed from Japanese and means ‘harbour wave’, although the waves do not occur only in harbours. The older term “tidal wave” is now out of favour, especially among scientists, since what causes a tsunami is unrelated to what causes the tides. “Seismic sea wave” is also used, since the waves are most often generated by seismic activity such as earthquakes. That term is not completely accurate either, because forces other than earthquakes can generate such waves by displacing water.

paragraphs.heading: Early records
paragraphs.text: The oldest tsunami in the human record struck the Greek colony of Potidaea in 479 BC. It is thought to have been triggered by an earthquake, and it may have spared the colony an invasion by the Achaemenid Empire. The Greek historian Thucydides was asking what causes tsunami as early as 426 BC, and nobody before him had argued that ocean earthquakes must be responsible. Later, the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus described the typical sequence after the 365 AD tsunami devastated Alexandria. First came an incipient earthquake, then the sea suddenly retreated, and then a gigantic wave followed.

paragraphs.heading: The toll
paragraphs.text: The impact of a tsunami is limited to coastal areas, but its destructive power can be enormous, and it can affect entire ocean basins. The Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004 ranks among the deadliest natural disasters in human history. At least 230,000 people were killed or went missing across 14 countries around that ocean. In the Mediterranean Sea and parts of Europe, tsunamis are a hazard that is often underestimated.

paragraphs.heading: Orphan tsunamis
paragraphs.text: Sometimes a tsunami cannot be linked to any earthquake, and it is then termed an “orphan tsunami”. This may happen with tsunamis from the distant past, before international communications, that were caused by earthquakes far away. One example is an earthquake in the Americas causing a tsunami in Japan.
